analysis.one_liner: Adds hearing aids and hearing care to Medicare coverage for beneficiaries with severe hearing loss.
analysis.headline: Two House committees approved the bill by voice vote, but the House never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare has long refused to pay for hearing aids, which are not considered medical treatment. This bill would have changed that: starting in 2022, Medicare Part B would cover hearing aids and hearing rehabilitation services for people with severe or profound hearing loss, with limits like one new hearing aid every five years and a written order from a physician or audiologist. It would also let audiologists bill Medicare directly and study whether patients could see an audiologist without a physician referral first.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries with severe or profound hearing loss, who today must pay out of pocket for hearing aids that often cost thousands of dollars. Audiologists and hearing aid providers would also gain a new source of covered business.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries with severe hearing loss

how_it_helps.text: Beginning January 1, 2022, Medicare Part B would cover aural rehabilitation and treatment services furnished by qualified audiologists [S5].
Medicare would pay for hearing aids for individuals diagnosed with profound or severe hearing loss, furnished on or after January 1, 2022 [S5].

Coverage is limited to one hearing aid per person per five-year period, only for prescription (not over-the-counter) hearing aid types, and only when furnished under a written order from a physician or qualified audiologist [S5].
Audiologists would be added to the list of practitioners who can be paid directly on an assignment-related basis for 2022 and later years [S5].

The Health and Human Services Inspector General would report within two years on whether audiologists could serve Medicare patients without referrals from physicians, and the Secretary could write rules to allow direct access if feasible [S5].
The bill was endorsed in committee by voice vote in both the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, indicating committee-level approval [S7].

analysis.who_pays: The Medicare Part B trust fund would pay for the new coverage, and the bill funds implementation by transferring money from the Federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund to CMS for 2020 through 2024. Medicare beneficiaries share in program costs through premiums, and hearing aid manufacturers and dispensers would be paid by Medicare for devices once beneficiaries covered out of pocket.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare's Part B trust fund and beneficiaries

drawbacks.text: Coverage is narrow: only people with severe or profound hearing loss qualify, they get one hearing aid every five years, and only prescription-style hearing aids are covered, not the cheaper over-the-counter devices the FDA has authorized [S5].
Adding hearing coverage increases spending from the Federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund, which is financed partly by beneficiary premiums [S5].
Payment is limited to hearing aids furnished under a written order of a physician or audiologist, so beneficiaries cannot simply purchase covered devices on their own [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors with profound hearing loss, hearing aids are a major out-of-pocket expense that Medicare has historically refused to cover at all, so the bill offered a real and concrete benefit. The costs are real too — new federal spending and higher premiums — and the design is conservative: a five-year limit, a severe-hearing-loss threshold, and a ban on covering over-the-counter devices all shrink the benefit and steer purchases toward the more expensive professionally fitted channel. A broader or better-targeted version might have covered more people at less cost per person.

outcome.mechanism: Both committees signed off on the bill and it was placed on the House calendar in January 2020, but the House never brought it up for a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced October 8, 2019 by Representative McBath, with Representative Dingell as an original cosponsor [S1][S5].
The Subcommittee on Health held hearings before the bill was even introduced, and the full Ways and Means Committee ordered it reported by voice vote in October 2019 [S7].
The committee bill was rewritten as a substitute and reported amended by Ways and Means on December 6, 2019 (H. Rept. 116-326, Part I) [S3][S7].
The Energy and Commerce Committee reported it on January 24, 2020 (H. Rept. 116-326, Part II), and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 302 [S4][S5][S7].
No further action was taken; the House never voted on the bill before the 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021 [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare beneficiaries with severe hearing loss gained nothing, and the Medicare program avoided the new spending. Hearing aid and audiology providers kept their business out of pocket rather than gaining a covered revenue stream, and physicians kept their role in ordering hearing aids.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody; the bill never got a vote

sides.party_line_note: Both committees approved the bill by voice vote, which masks the party split, and only six Democrats cosponsored it; no floor vote ever recorded an on-the-record position.

industries.note: Medicare coverage would have made hearing aids a covered benefit, creating a large new paying customer base. The bill excludes over-the-counter hearing aids from coverage and requires a professional written order, which channels purchases to the more expensive fitted-and-dispensed products rather than cheaper self-purchased devices.

Audiologists would become directly payable Medicare practitioners in 2022 and beyond, and a study and possible rules would let patients come to them without physician referrals, expanding their patient base.

Physicians keep the right to order covered hearing aids and to furnish dispensing under an exemption from competitive acquisition, but the bill directs a study of letting audiologists see Medicare patients without physician referrals, which would erode that gatekeeping role over time.

industries.industry: Medicare Part B (Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund)
industries.note: The trust fund would pay for newly covered hearing aids and services plus implementation costs transferred to CMS for 2020 through 2024, with beneficiaries sharing through premiums.
